title: Are ODI Teams Attacking Too Late?
subtitle: Why overs 31–40 may deserve a rethink after the ICC's rule change.
description: Why overs 31–40 may deserve a rethink after the ICC's rule change.
blocks: **Sport is full of strategies that seem obvious, until someone asks whether they are actually optimal.**

Baseball went through exactly that rethink. For years, starting pitchers were expected to work deep into games, and managers usually waited for visible trouble before replacing them. Then the data began showing that hitters became increasingly successful each time they faced the same starter.

Now, instead of asking *how long is a starter supposed to pitch?*, teams began asking *where is he actually most valuable?* That small change in thinking eventually changed how pitching resources were used.
I think ODI cricket may have one of those moments sitting right in front of us.
Why overs 31–40 may deserve a rethink after the ICC’s latest rule change.

With the ICC’s new single-ball rule for the final 16 overs, **overs 31–40** have become the **last free-scoring period** in an ODI innings. Although, the 2nd Powerplay comprises overs 11 to 40, with at most 4 fielders allowed outside the circle, the overs 31 to 40 phase has certainly shown some characteristics, which I will explain shortly, that are different than the 20 over phase before them with the same field restrictions.

This window of last 10 overs before the fielding side gets extra fielder outside the circle appears to be a Batting Powerplay, but most teams haven’t adjusted so far. With another ODI World Cup approaching, that could matter.
So, Who Are We Actually Waiting to Attack?
There is a reason I keep coming back to overs 31–40. On paper, there is nothing particularly special about this ten-over block, but look at **who is actually bowling it**.

Since 2019, the distribution of bowling overs changes quite noticeably once an innings reaches the **31st** over. The first and second bowling options, the bowlers captains rely on most, see their involvement drop. Meanwhile, the fourth, fifth and sixth options take on a much bigger share.

The fifth bowling option alone bowls **19.3%** of all deliveries in this phase, more than any other bowling option. The sixth option contributes another **16.5%**. This is a very different bowling environment from the first 30 overs.

*Figure 1. Share of deliveries bowled by each bowling option in men’s ODIs since 2019. The distribution shifts towards the weaker bowling options during overs 31–40, before moving sharply back towards the frontline bowlers at the death.*

I think there is a fairly simple reason for this. A captain has 50 overs to find from his attack. The fifth and sixth options, often an all-rounder or someone in the side who isn’t primarily there for his bowling, have to get their overs in somewhere. Overs 31–40 appear to be where a lot of those overs are being found.
If I group the first four bowling options together and compare them with options five and six, the difference becomes even clearer.
*Figure 2. Combined usage of bowling options 1–4 and 5–6 across an ODI innings. Overs 31–40 provide the greatest exposure to the fifth and sixth bowling options.*
Options five and six bowl just **24.8%** of deliveries in the first 30 overs. During overs 31–40, that jumps to **35.8%**. By the final ten, it is back down to **23.2%**.
So, for ten overs, more than **one in every three balls** is coming from the fifth or sixth bowling option.
Now this is where it gets interesting for me.
If this is the phase where batting sides get their greatest access to the secondary bowlers, surely we should see them being attacked?
*Figure 3. Combined run rates conceded by the first two and fifth/sixth bowling options. Despite their increased exposure in overs 31–40, the secondary options concede just 5.35 runs per over.*

The fifth and sixth bowling options concede at only **5.35 runs per over** between overs **31 and 40.** For the phase where these bowlers are at their most exposed, with only four fielders allowed outside the circle, that feels remarkably low. Move further into the innings and the same category of bowlers concedes **6.17 per over**. In the final five, it shoots up to **8.23.**

Teams are clearly willing to take more risk later. Once they get towards the final ten, and especially the final five, everyone knows what is coming. They’ll throw their bats at everything in the final 5.
But why wait? Think about the trade-off.
In overs 31–40, I can potentially attack the fifth or sixth bowling option while there are **only four fielders outside the circle**.
If I wait until overs 41–50, the fielding side gets another boundary rider.

And if I wait even longer, until the final five, I am increasingly likely to be facing the bowlers the opposition captain has specifically saved for that job. And, if it reverses, which it can due to the new rule, it’ll be even more difficult to hit.

So we seem to have arrived at this slightly strange situation where batting teams are being given perhaps their best combination of **bowler access and fielding restrictions**, and are still treating the period relatively conservatively. I think there are runs being left here.
So, Who Is Actually Using This Window?
If overs 31–40 really are giving batting teams something extra, then the obvious next question is: **who has actually figured it out?**
I looked at how the ten teams from the 2023 World Cup have batted in this phase since the start of 2023. And there isn’t one common approach. In fact, the differences are quite revealing.
*Figure 4. Overall strike rate against non-boundary strike rate in overs 31–40 since 2023. Bubble size represents batting average.*

India, for example, have the highest non-boundary strike rate of the ten teams. England score faster overall, but India keep the innings moving better when the boundary isn’t there. Pakistan aren’t far behind on either measure.
That matters in this phase. I don’t think attacking overs 31–40 simply means hitting more fours and sixes. The better version is being able to push the baseline up even between boundaries.
The risk side tells another story.
*Figure 5. Balls per boundary against balls per dismissal in overs 31–40. Moving towards the top-left represents more frequent boundaries while losing fewer wickets.*

India are almost on their own here. They find a boundary roughly every 9.6 balls, but lose a wicket only once every **41.6 balls**. England find boundaries even more frequently, while Pakistan, New Zealand and South Africa sit in a similar attacking cluster.
But the fourth graph is the one I find most interesting.

Remember what we established in the previous section. **This is the phase where the fifth and sixth bowling options are most exposed.** So forget overall scoring for a moment. What happens when teams face *those two bowlers specifically*? Now the separation becomes much clearer.
*Figure 6. Strike rate and batting average against the fifth and sixth bowling options during overs 31–40.*
Pakistan have probably been the closest to what I am talking about. Against options five and six, they score at a strike rate of **107.6 while averaging 47**.

England are at **104.8 and 44.5**. India score slightly slower at **101.2**, but average an outstanding **51.1**. New Zealand are aggressive too, striking at almost 104, although they lose wickets more often.

That top-right part of the graph is where I would want to be. But then look at everyone else. Australia strike at just **91.9** against the fifth and sixth options. South Africa, despite being one of the better overall scoring sides in this phase, are below 100 against them. Sri Lanka are at 93.0. Afghanistan, Netherlands and Bangladesh fall even further away.
So, Are ODI Teams Attacking Too Late?

Think about ENG vs IND’s Lords’ ODI, IND had made a small comeback with the ball in the 31-40 phase picking wickets and not allowing ENG openers to whack the ball. When the 1st wicket fell, I was surprised to see Joe Root coming out to bat. Better strategy could’ve been sending an enforcing batter before Root, on that day, which might have increased the scoring rate. It felt like ENG left many runs on the field, however due to death bowling weakness Buttler outrageously scored in the final 4 overs. But, this won’t happen everyday. This mistake from them might have actually led to India winning the series.

These aren’t the overs where I would be happy simply getting through at five or five-and-a-half an over. If the fifth bowler has overs left, I want to face those overs now. If the sixth option comes on, I don’t want to wait for over 46 to decide that it is time to attack because by then, the game has changed. There is another fielder outside the circle. The frontline bowlers are coming back. And under the new ball rule, waiting may become even less rewarding. Even among the best teams, I don’t think anyone has completely maxed it out yet.
And there is another benefit which won’t necessarily appear in the run-rate graph.
Suppose I attack your fifth bowler in the 33rd over and your sixth bowler in the 35th. Suddenly, you have a decision to make.
Do you let me continue attacking the matchup?
Or do you bring one of your best bowlers back?

If you choose the second option, I have already achieved something. **I have made you spend a resource earlier than you wanted to.** An over from your best bowler in the 36th is one fewer over he can bowl when I am trying to launch at the end.
That is why I don’t see overs 31–40 as simply another chunk of the middle overs anymore. I almost see it as a Batting Powerplay hiding in plain sight.
